transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-06-17
- Start time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~45 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Dan Rivera (AtlasAI ML), Priya Singh (AtlasAI Infra), Tom Cho (AtlasAI CTO)

Summary:
Quick sync on the current POC runs — review of last week's TTFT numbers, new microburst results, discussion about tradeoffs for kernel selection under mixed seqlen traffic, and action items to validate on-prem smoke test. Some transcription noise; a few product names autofilled as 'Redwood Optima' in notes.

Topics:
- TTFT baseline vs optimized
- Streaming handshake and first-token strategies
- Sequence length distribution and KV cache behavior
- Kernel selection (fastpath vs stable vs quantized int8)
- Microburst and hedging strategies

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: thanks everyone for joining, we'll keep this tight 45 min ish, last week's numbers were pretty encouraging but a couple of microburst spikes popped up so Arjun and I wanted to run through root causes and next steps.
[00:18] Dan: yeah thanks, we're seeing the TTFT p50 at about 75ms on the fastpath but p95 jumps to 340ms sometimes, those are the spikes we care about.
[00:34] Arjun: right so baseline for the model on Redwood Dedicated we measured p50 ~78ms, p95 ~210ms in controlled lab, but once you throw in your production-like mix with long seqlens and shared autoscale we get those microbursts.
[00:52] Priya: to be clear our traffic mixes about 65% short queries (<=128 tokens) and 20% mid (129-512) and then that 15% tail that goes up to 1k. we also have a small steady stream of 2-3 long batched ops that coincide with consumer batch windows. could that batching be interfering with the TTFT?
[01:15] Arjun: yes, batching + autoscale warmups + KV cache churn can compound. when the KV cache misses for long sequences we do more attention compute and a different kernel path, that pushes latency. also we saw a couple of requests get routed to a different model variant — fallback to the stable-quantized variant — that added 80-120ms.
[01:36] Tom: fallback happened automatically? that's worrying for predictability.
[01:40] Maya: it's configured as a capacity fallback policy — if the fastpath GPU pool is saturated we fallback to a compatible variant to keep requests served. the tradeoff is increased latency but preserved availability. we can tighten hedging windows or reserve dedicated capacity to avoid that.
[01:58] Dan: what about streaming first-byte? a lot of our UX is sensitive to first-token latency.
[02:03] Arjun: the streaming handshake adds small overhead; our recent experiment with early-token flush (we called it 'fast-write' in the notes) brought first-token down by ~30ms on average. however with microbursts those improvements disappear for the tail.
[02:22] Dan: numbers?
[02:24] Arjun: current TF/TTFT baseline: p50 first-token 60-80ms, optimized handshake ~28-45ms, but in microburst windows we saw first-token spike to 250-400ms.
[02:37] Priya: are those spikes correlated with sequence-length distribution?
[02:40] Arjun: yes strongly. when we get concurrent long sequences, the kernel selector shifts to a memory-heavy kernel that's not as optimized for streaming. that kernel also can't use the same KV cache efficiently, so you get extra mem copies.
[02:54] Maya: two levers here: 1) routing policy — split short/long into separate pools so long seqs don't affect short fastpath, 2) kernel-level optimization — choose a different kernel or quantization profile for mid-length sequences to balance throughput and latency.
[03:12] Tom: how invasive is splitting pools? our infra team prefers fewer pools but predictable SLAs.
[03:19] Priya: we can do segregated pools but it costs ops overhead; we need to quantify cost
[03:24] Maya: understood — that's why we suggested a small dedicated pool for short fastpath traffic (cheap GPUs or lower batch sizes) to keep first-token SLO without heavy spend. we can show cost delta in a single slide.
[03:40] Dan: last week's kernel swap where you tried fastpath kernel v3, it improved p50 but p95 degraded. can you recap what changed?
[03:49] Arjun: sure — fastpath v3 uses a fused attention kernel optimized for short seqlen with aggressive register tiling. it's excellent for <=128 tokens. but when requests >512 concurrently, its resource use increases and you hit contention — p95 suffers. the stablekernel variant uses less aggressive tiling and is more predictable across mixed seqlen.
[04:12] Maya: we also tried quantized int8 (note: sometimes transcribed as 'int-eight') variants — those save ~30% compute and cost but introduced some jitter in our microburst runs. not huge quality regressions but enough to push p95.
[04:27] Dan: so options are: accept the jitter and save cost, or run segregated pools, or try dynamic kernel swapping per-request — does Redwood support per-request kernel hints?
[04:38] Arjun: we have per-request runtime hints, yes. you can tag routes and prefer a kernel family. but switching kernels frequently has its own overhead if it's not pre-warmed. that's where caching and the smart router come in — keep a warm set of kernels for expected distributions.
[04:56] Priya: is there an automated way to detect microburst onset and spin up a hedged path? we prefer automation over manual rule tuning.
[05:03] Arjun: we have a hedging policy prototype — it watches p95 trends and can route a fraction to an alternate pool within milliseconds. for the POC it's not production-locked but we can enable a controlled version.
[05:16] Dan: ok cool. earlier you mentioned KV cache churn — can you explain what that is in plain terms?
[05:21] Arjun: sure, when you stream tokens and keep KV cached, repeated contexts reuse that memory. if we have many long unique contexts the cache evicts and you get misses, so later tokens require full recompute instead of cheap cache lookups. that's the churn we mean.
[05:36] Maya: the Atlas prompt distribution Dan will send will help us estimate cache hit rates and recommend a cache size and pooling strategy.
[05:44] Tom: on-prem concerns — Priya will we be able to open the port for Redwood smoke runner? there's a short window next week.
[05:51] Priya: yeah we'll confirm, but need an IP allowlist and the test runner is ephemeral. I want to ensure logs don't leak. we also need the SOC2 docs again.
[06:02] Maya: got it, I'll attach SOC2 and the infra checklist in the follow-up email.
[06:06] Dan: quick question about the 'fallback variant' you said earlier — can we pin routes to avoid auto-fallback? we just want controlled fallbacks.
[06:14] Arjun: yes routes can pin model versions or disable fallback. default pilot config had fallback enabled to preserve availability, but we can turn it off for production-critical routes.
[06:24] Tom: cost question — what's the rough delta for segregated short-pool vs single shared pool?
[06:29] Maya: rough ballpark — segregated short pool with small instances pushes cost up ~12-18% in our sims but improves first-token p95 dramatically. exact numbers we'll send in the pricing sheet.
[06:40] Dan: about microburst tests — what's the exact pattern you want us to run?
[06:45] Arjun: please do stepped qps: 100 sustained for 10min, 1k for 10min, 10k for 5min bursts, with a mixed seqlen distribution matching your histogram. repeat twice to catch warmup effects. also include a phase with 30% of requests pinned to long seqlen to observe cache churn.
[07:07] Priya: we'll do that and also isolate a window for on-prem smoke.
[07:11] Maya: excellent. next steps also include Arjun posting the microburst CSV into the shared drive and Maya emailing the SOC2 and benchmark dashboard.
[07:22] Dan: any blockers today from Redwood side?
[07:25] Arjun: none other than needing Atlas prompt hist and a greenlit test window.
[07:30] Tom: timeline — if microburst looks good and p95 improves with segregated pool, we can look at a reserved capacity commit in July.
[07:38] Maya: perfect — I'll follow up with pricing options and a proposed commit slider.
[07:44] Dan: one last nit — can you call out which kernels produced the highest jitter in the spreadsheet? it helps our infra prioritize.
[07:50] Arjun: yes we'll annotate: fastpath-v3 (high jitter when >512 concurrent long), stablekernel-2 (predictable), quant-int8-beta (cost saving but occasional p95 spikes).
[07:59] Maya: thanks all, recap and action items in the follow-up. any final questions?
[08:04] Priya: none from me.
[08:05] Tom: nope.
[08:06] Dan: good, thanks.
[08:08] Maya: thanks team — end call.
